We introduce a novel concept removal method for frontier diffusion and image autoregressive models, such as SD3.5, Flux, and Infinity. Our intervention replaces the internal bottleneck layer present in all these modern models with a transcoder that is trained to replicate the original layer while structuring it into distinct activation features. This in-place substitution creates an integrated filter through which concept-specific signals can be selectively disabled while preserving the rest of the model's behavior. Since the intervention modifies the model backbone rather than attaching an external component, it remains persistent under white-box access. Empirically, the approach achieves state-of-the-art concept removal performance across modern diffusion and autoregressive models, maintains visual generation quality, provides robustness against adversarial prompts, and supports sequential removal of diverse concepts. This positions our method as a practical approach for concept removal in frontier image generative models.

Artificial intelligence increasingly drives automated scientific discovery, yet contemporary generalist agents lack physical grounding, frequently hallucinating hardware-incompatible designs. Here, we present a physically grounded, multi-agent discovery engine that autonomously architects hardware-compliant computing systems. Anchored by an Evolutionary Knowledge Graph structuring past scientific innovations, the framework extracts an "algorithmic Chain-of-Thought" to transform blind stochastic search into directed structural evolution. Applied to the extreme testbed of foundation model deployment, the engine evolved two hardware-aware compression methodologies surpassing human-engineered heuristics: Q-Enhance mitigates long-context accuracy loss in dense models, and MoE-Salient-AQ outperforms state-of-the-art manual sparse Mixture-of-Experts designs by 3.7% at sub-3-bit regimes. Utilizing a bandwidth-efficient Sensitivity Profile, we successfully deployed a massive 235-billion-parameter model onto a constrained dual-A100 server, reducing memory requirements by 75% with a marginal 0.64% accuracy degradation. By transforming unconstrained combinatorial search into knowledge-driven autonomy, this establishes a scalable hardware-software co-design paradigm for machine-driven discovery within strict physical boundaries.

Online reinforcement learning (RL) agents increasingly depend on knowledge acquired offline to achieve practical efficiency. Originally studied in offline-to-online RL, this paradigm now spans foundation model post-training and embodied intelligence, with prior types expanding from offline datasets and pre-trained policies to increasingly diverse knowledge sources such as multimodal foundation models and generative world models. Offline priors have become central to how deep RL is developed and deployed. However, this reliance introduces a challenge that the prevailing benchmark-driven paradigm cannot resolve: because prior validity varies across deployments and shifts during training, no single approach to managing it is universally optimal, and benchmark rankings offer limited guidance for real-world deployments. Rather than pursuing universal solutions, we argue that the field should shift to diagnosis-driven tension management, in which deployment-specific evidence guides how the learner relates to its priors throughout training, enabling both flexible and adaptive deployment. We support this position with a framework characterizing how priors reshape online optimization through three functional roles, controlled experiments demonstrating help-or-hurt reversals, cross-domain evidence from foundation model post-training to embodied intelligence, and engagement with five substantive counterarguments.

Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning assumes each agent shares the same reward function and can be trained effectively using the Trust Region framework of single-agent. Instead of relying on other agents' actions, the independent actors setting considers each agent to act based only on its local information, thus having more flexible applications. However, in the sequential update framework, it is required to re-estimate the joint advantage function after each individual agent's policy step. Despite the practical success of importance sampling, the updated advantage function suffers from exponentially high variance problems, which likely result in unstable convergence. In this work, we first analyze the high variance advantage both empirically and theoretically. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a clipping objective to control the upper bounds of the advantage fluctuation in sequential updates. With the proposed objective, we provide a monotonic bound with sub-linear convergence to $ε$-Nash Equilibria. We further derive two new practical algorithms using our clipping objective. The experiment results on three popular multi-agent reinforcement learning benchmarks show that our proposed method outperforms the tested baselines in most environments. By carefully analyzing different training settings, our proposed method is highlighted with both stable convergence properties and the desired low advantage variance estimation. For reproducibility purposes, our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/giangbang/Low-Variance-Trust-Region-MARL.

Quantization is widely used to reduce the inference cost of large language models, but its effect on reasoning models is not fully captured by final-answer accuracy or per-token latency. We show that low-bit post-training quantization can introduce a hidden test-time compute cost: quantized reasoning models often generate longer chains of thought even when they still answer correctly. Across mathematical reasoning, code generation, scientific question answering, and agentic tool-use benchmarks, we find that INT4/INT3 quantization can preserve accuracy but increase reasoning-token usage, offsetting the expected per-token speedup. To measure this effect, we introduce the CoT Token Inflation Ratio, which compares reasoning length between quantized and full-precision models averaged across all evaluation benchmarks. We further show that token inflation is accompanied by behavioral changes in the reasoning trace, including more intermediate steps and greater semantic repetition. These changes translate into measurable end-to-end real-world serving penalties. Finally, we evaluate mitigation strategies and find that prompting and decoding-time sampling offer inconsistent accuracy-length trade-offs, while quantization-aware training shows more promise in reducing both accuracy degradation and token inflation. Our results suggest that reasoning-token usage should be reported alongside accuracy when evaluating quantized reasoning models.

Knowledge Distillation (KD) is widely used to obtain compact models for efficient inference in resource-constrained environments. Yet the computational overhead of the distillation process itself is often overlooked, raising the question of whether a better student model can be obtained with less data and less compute via data pruning. However, existing data pruning methods are not designed for KD: some introduce substantial overhead, such as obtaining training dynamics through retraining, while others rely on heuristic selection rules that fail to capture what KD actually requires, often resulting in suboptimal subsets. To address these issues, we propose IF-Beta, an efficient data pruning framework that combines influence functions with a learnable sampling policy. Empirically, we first demonstrate that influence functions can serve as an effective and efficient estimator of sample impact in KD settings, where only a pretrained teacher is available. Building on this, our sampling policy is specifically parameterized by a Beta distribution, whose highly flexible two-parameter family allows the policy to adapt to diverse pruning regimes rather than being tied to fixed heuristic forms. Next, we formulate KD pruning as optimizing this policy through a bilevel objective, where the inner loop operates in the teacher feature space with a KD-aligned objective, enabling fast proxy training, while the outer loop updates the policy parameters to maximize distillation performance. This design ensures that IF-Beta is both computationally efficient and inherently aligned with the goals of KD. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet show that IF-Beta consistently outperforms other baselines across a wide range of pruning ratios. Remarkably, IF-Beta enables students trained on less data and less compute to surpass the performance of students distilled on the full dataset.

Almost every paper on LLM jailbreaks and prompt injection reports an attack-success rate (ASR), and that number is assigned not by people but by an automated judge: either a safety classifier trained for the task, or a general chat model prompted to grade. The judge is rarely checked. We check it. Using 596 human-labeled completions from the HarmBench classifier validation set, we compare the two judge families against human majority votes and then attack them. The two families fail in opposite ways. The dedicated classifier over-flags (precision 0.835, recall 0.974); three different LLM-as-judges keep high precision (0.81 to 0.94) but show erratic recall (0.06 to 0.65), so the same responses produce very different ASR depending on which judge scores them. The two families also differ sharply in robustness. Wrappers that leave the harmful text untouched and only add benign framing flip every LLM-judge between 57% and 100% of the time, and a single prepended refusal sentence accounts for much of this (39% to 88%). The dedicated classifier resists these surface attacks (at most 6.7%), but a white-box GCG attack on its open weights flips 70% of confident true positives (21 of 30; 95% CI 54 to 86%) even at a small optimization budget. A two-annotator audit confirms the attacks leave the harm intact: every one of 80 sampled flips still contained the harmful content. Because a large and growing share of reported ASR comes from LLM-judges, many such numbers are unreliable both on average and under deliberate pressure. We recommend that papers report judge precision and recall on a human-labeled slice, report ASR corrected for judge precision, and include an adversarial check of the judge. Our code is released.

**Abstract**

This paper examines the fundamental distinction between auditory signal processing and genuine listening in contemporary real-time voice-based artificial intelligence systems. While current voice AI demonstrates remarkable proficiency in transcribing, parsing, and responding to spoken language with low latency, we argue that such systems fundamentally *hear* without *listening*. Listening implies a dynamic, contextual, and ethically engaged process of understanding that incorporates intent, emotional nuance, and conversational memory. Through a series of controlled experiments comparing human-human interactions with human-AI dialogues using state-of-the-art voice interfaces, we demonstrate that real-time voice AI exhibits three critical failures: (1) an inability to differentiate between literal content and pragmatic intent, (2) a systematic neglect of paralinguistic cues such as tone and hesitation, and (3) a structural amnesia that prevents genuine contextual coherence beyond immediate turns. We propose a theoretical framework—*auditory functionalism*—to characterize this disparity, where AI processes speech as a data stream optimized for response generation rather than as a relational act. The findings challenge the prevailing assumption that real-time voice interaction equates to conversational intelligence. We conclude that achieving authentic listening in AI requires not merely faster processing, but a paradigm shift toward modeling the ethical, temporal, and affective dimensions of human discourse.

**Abstract:** Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed to interpret and reason over complex data, yet their reliability under varying analytical conditions remains underexplored. This paper introduces the concept of *auditing order sensitivity*—the susceptibility of MLLMs to produce inconsistent answers when the same set of evidence is presented in different sequential orders. We systematically investigate this phenomenon across a diverse suite of state-of-the-art MLLMs, including proprietary and open-source variants, using a novel benchmark of multimodal reasoning tasks. Our experiments reveal a pervasive and significant order sensitivity: models frequently alter their final responses, confidence levels, and intermediate reasoning steps solely due to the permutation of input evidence, even when the underlying semantic content is identical. We quantify this variability and demonstrate that it is not merely a reflection of task difficulty but is tied to the models' attention mechanisms and positional encoding biases. Further, we show that this sensitivity can be exploited to artificially inflate or deflate perceived model accuracy on curated test sets. Our findings expose a critical fragility in MLLM reasoning, underscoring the need for auditing protocols that account for input order invariance and raising fundamental questions about the robustness of their claimed multimodal understanding.

**Abstract**
This paper introduces and examines *keyword lexicon blindness*—a methodological artifact wherein automated text analysis tools systematically misidentify rhetorical stance due to the rigid, context-independent application of predefined keyword dictionaries. We argue that reliance on fixed lexicons for detecting certainty, affect, and epistemic stance conflates linguistic form with pragmatic function, leading to significant measurement error, particularly in domains where rhetorical nuance is paramount. Through a series of computational experiments and qualitative discourse analysis, we demonstrate how standard sentiment and stance-detection lexicons fail to distinguish between genuine conviction and strategic hedging, ironic certainty, or performative assertiveness. Our findings reveal that up to 30% of stance classifications in political and legal corpora are artifacts of lexical matching rather than accurate representations of speaker intention. We propose a corrective framework integrating contextual embedding disambiguation and discourse-aware weighting to mitigate this blindness. The paper concludes that without such corrections, computational rhetoric risks measuring not the certainty of the speaker, but the certainty of the tool's own lexical assumptions. We urge a methodological shift toward hybrid approaches that treat lexicons as probabilistic guides rather than deterministic classifiers, thereby rescuing the measurement of rhetorical stance from its current artifact-driven distortions.

**Abstract**  
We introduce *natural ungrokking*, a phenomenon in which neural networks, during standard pretraining on natural data, asymmetrically forget or suppress certain learned rules while retaining others, without explicit regularization or task-specific fine-tuning. Unlike synthetic grokking scenarios—where delayed generalization emerges under limited data—natural ungrokking arises from the statistical structure of real-world corpora: rules that are statistically frequent, contextually redundant, or aligned with the training distribution’s latent manifold are preserved, whereas rare, ambiguous, or conflicting rules are spontaneously discarded. Through controlled experiments on transformer language models and vision models, we demonstrate that this asymmetric control emerges from the interplay of gradient dynamics, implicit regularization via stochastic optimization, and the inherent competition between predictive features. We further show that the surviving rules are not merely those with higher raw frequency, but those that minimize the model’s long-term prediction error under the natural distribution’s noise. Our findings suggest that pretraining inherently imposes a form of rule selection—an implicit curriculum that prioritizes generalizable, low-complexity patterns over spurious or idiosyncratic ones. This has implications for understanding generalization in foundation models, designing more robust training regimes, and explaining why certain biases persist while others are naturally unlearned.

**Abstract**  
Vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in optical character recognition (OCR) and subsequent reasoning tasks, yet their robustness under real-world visual perturbations remains underexplored. This paper systematically evaluates the OCR-reasoning robustness of state-of-the-art VLMs against diverse visual perturbations, including geometric distortions (rotation, scaling, shearing), photometric degradations (blur, noise, brightness variation), and structural occlusions (partial masking, adversarial patches). We introduce a benchmark suite comprising perturbed versions of standard OCR-reasoning datasets, spanning text-based question answering, mathematical expression recognition, and document analysis. Through extensive experiments on models such as CLIP, Flamingo, and GPT-4V, we find that performance degrades significantly—often by over 30%—under mild perturbations that leave human readability intact. Notably, reasoning accuracy is disproportionately affected by perturbations that disrupt character adjacency and spatial layout, even when individual characters remain recognizable. We further analyze model sensitivity to perturbation intensity and type, revealing that current VLMs lack robust visual grounding for OCR-reasoning tasks, relying heavily on pristine visual input. Our findings highlight critical vulnerabilities in deploying VLMs for real-world OCR-reasoning applications and underscore the need for perturbation-invariant architectures and training strategies. This work establishes a foundation for developing more resilient multimodal reasoning systems.

**Abstract**  
While artificial intelligence (AI) has achieved remarkable fluency in machine translation, its application to literary texts remains a subject of debate. This study investigates reader preferences between AI-generated and human translations of literary works, focusing on stylistic nuance, emotional resonance, and cultural fidelity. Through a mixed-methods experiment, 120 participants evaluated excerpts from contemporary fiction translated by both AI (GPT-4, fine-tuned for literary style) and professional human translators. Quantitative ratings revealed that AI translations were judged as “fine”—acceptable in terms of literal accuracy and grammatical correctness. However, qualitative analysis and preference surveys indicated a significant bias toward human translations, particularly for elements such as idiomatic expression, rhythm, character voice, and metaphorical depth. Readers consistently reported that human translations “felt more natural” and preserved the author’s unique stylistic signature, even when AI output was syntactically flawless. Further, the emotional impact of passages was rated significantly higher in human-translated versions. These findings suggest that while AI has achieved a threshold of basic adequacy for literary translation, it fails to replicate the interpretive artistry and cultural sensitivity that readers value. The study underscores that for literary texts, reader satisfaction hinges not on mere accuracy but on perceived authenticity and aesthetic coherence—qualities that, for now, remain the domain of human translators.

**Abstract:**  
Text summarization models are increasingly vulnerable to data poisoning attacks, where maliciously crafted training samples can degrade model performance or induce targeted misbehavior. Existing defenses often rely on static filtering or anomaly detection, which fail to adapt to evolving attack strategies and overlook subtle poisoning cues. We propose a three-stage defense framework—Detect, Unlearn, Restore—that systematically identifies, neutralizes, and recovers from data poisoning in abstractive and extractive summarization systems. In the Detect phase, we leverage a lightweight auxiliary classifier trained on model confidence and attention patterns to flag suspicious training instances. The Unlearn phase employs a gradient-based forgetting mechanism that selectively removes the influence of flagged poisoned samples without full retraining. Finally, the Restore phase applies a targeted fine-tuning procedure on a clean subset to repair residual performance degradation. Extensive experiments on multiple summarization datasets and poisoning scenarios (including backdoor triggers and summary-length manipulation) demonstrate that our method reduces attack success rate by over 85% while preserving summary coherence and factual accuracy. The framework introduces minimal computational overhead and generalizes across transformer-based architectures. Our work provides a robust, proactive defense pipeline for securing text summarization against adversarial data poisoning.

**Abstract**
Multi-step tool-use reinforcement learning (RL) enables agents to solve complex tasks by leveraging external tools, yet it frequently collapses into inefficient or incoherent behavior, such as tool overuse, action chaining failures, or catastrophic forgetting. This paper identifies the root cause of this collapse: the compounding effect of sparse, delayed, and noisy rewards in long-horizon tool-use trajectories, which undermines gradient stability and leads to policy degeneration. We formally characterize the collapse as a loss of temporal credit assignment coherence, where the agent fails to distinguish effective tool-use sequences from random perturbations. To address this, we introduce Supervisory Signals—auxiliary loss functions derived from tool-use metadata, including tool-switch penalties, stepwise progress indicators, and task-relevant subgoal completion cues. These signals provide dense, structured feedback that preserves the temporal dependencies critical for multi-step reasoning. Through extensive experiments on simulated tool-use environments (e.g., block manipulation and API-based retrieval tasks), we demonstrate that supervisory signals stabilize policy gradients, reduce collapse rates by over 60%, and improve task success rates from 45% to 89%. Our findings reveal that the collapse is not an inherent limitation of RL for tool-use but a symptom of inadequate reward shaping, and that supervisory signals offer a principled, scalable fix. This work advances the understanding of tool-use RL and provides actionable guidelines for robust agent design.

**Abstract**  
This paper introduces Tatoxa, a novel system designed for text detoxification in low-resource languages, with a focus on Tatar (Tatarstan, Russia). Text detoxification—the task of converting offensive or toxic language into neutral, polite equivalents—remains underdeveloped for languages with limited digital corpora and computational resources. We address this gap by presenting a modular pipeline combining a lightweight toxicity classifier, a rule-based normalization module, and a fine-tuned sequence-to-sequence model adapted from a multilingual pre-trained transformer (mT5). To overcome data scarcity, we curate a parallel corpus of 12,000 Tatar sentences annotated for toxicity and neutral rewrites, augmented through back-translation and lexical substitution strategies. Tatoxa achieves 87.3% accuracy in toxicity detection and 79.1% in detoxification quality (human-evaluated fluency and meaning preservation), outperforming direct translation-based baselines by over 15 points. We further analyze challenges unique to Tatar, including agglutinative morphology and code-switching with Russian, and propose lightweight adaptation strategies applicable to other low-resource languages. The Tatoxa system demonstrates that targeted, resource-efficient approaches can achieve robust detoxification outcomes even in severely under-resourced linguistic contexts, offering a scalable blueprint for computational sociolinguistic intervention in minority languages.

**Abstract**  
This paper presents Dziri Voicebot, the first end-to-end, low-resource speech-to-speech conversational system designed specifically for the Algerian dialect. Addressing the scarcity of annotated corpora and the phonological complexity of Algerian Arabic, we propose a cascaded architecture integrating automatic speech recognition (ASR), neural machine translation, and text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis, all trained on a newly collected dataset of 120 hours of spontaneous dialectal speech. To mitigate data sparsity, we employ cross-lingual transfer learning from Modern Standard Arabic and multilingual pretrained models, followed by iterative fine-tuning with synthetic data augmentation. Our ASR module achieves a word error rate of 18.7% on unseen dialectal recordings, while the TTS component produces natural-sounding speech with a mean opinion score of 3.9 out of 5. The conversational pipeline operates with an average end-to-end latency of 2.3 seconds on a single GPU, making it viable for real-time deployment. Dziri Voicebot demonstrates that high-quality dialectal speech interaction is achievable with limited resources, paving the way for inclusive voice interfaces in underrepresented languages. The system is released as an open-source prototype to foster further research in North African dialect processing.

**Abstract:**  
The generation of high-quality synthetic data is critical for addressing data scarcity, privacy concerns, and class imbalance in machine learning. However, existing approaches often require extensive manual tuning, domain expertise, or iterative human-in-the-loop processes, limiting scalability and reproducibility. We introduce **Autodata**, an agentic data scientist framework that autonomously creates realistic, task-specific synthetic datasets. Autodata leverages a large language model (LLM)-driven agent to iteratively analyze a target dataset, infer its statistical and structural characteristics, and orchestrate a suite of generative models—including variational autoencoders, generative adversarial networks, and diffusion-based methods—to produce synthetic samples. The agent employs a self-reflective loop: it generates candidate data, evaluates fidelity against user-defined metrics (e.g., distributional similarity, feature correlations, and downstream utility), and refines its strategy through prompt-based feedback. Crucially, Autodata incorporates a novel “data scientist” persona that automatically selects appropriate generation techniques, tunes hyperparameters, and validates outputs without human intervention. In extensive experiments across tabular, image, and time-series domains, Autodata consistently outperforms static generation pipelines and manual baselines, achieving higher fidelity and downstream model accuracy while reducing human effort by over 80%. Our work establishes a paradigm shift toward autonomous, agent-driven synthetic data generation, democratizing access to high-quality data for robust machine learning.

**Abstract**

This paper introduces SpeechEQ, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate the Emotional Intelligence Quotient (EQ) of socially aware voice conversational models. While recent advances in text-based dialogue systems have made significant strides in understanding and generating empathetic responses, the unique acoustic and prosodic dimensions of spoken interactions—such as tone, pitch, and speaking rate—remain underexplored in evaluation frameworks. SpeechEQ addresses this gap by establishing a multi-modal evaluation protocol that assesses a model’s ability to perceive, interpret, and appropriately respond to emotional cues in spoken conversations. The benchmark comprises four core tasks: Emotion Recognition from Speech, Contextual Empathy Scoring, Prosodic Appropriateness Judgment, and Adaptive Response Generation. We evaluate a diverse set of state-of-the-art voice models, including both end-to-end spoken systems and cascaded text-to-speech architectures. Our findings reveal a significant discrepancy between a model’s textual EQ and its spoken EQ, with many systems failing to modulate vocal delivery based on detected emotional context. Furthermore, we identify that prosodic alignment with user affect is a stronger predictor of user satisfaction than lexical accuracy alone. SpeechEQ provides a standardized framework for future research, highlighting critical areas for improvement in building truly emotionally intelligent voice conversational agents.

**Abstract**

This paper introduces "Weave of Formal Thought," a conceptual framework for modeling the interleaving of intuitive and analytical reasoning in complex problem-solving. Moving beyond traditional stage-based models of cognition, we propose that formal logic and heuristic insight are not sequential but co-articulated, forming a dynamic fabric where each thread of deduction is interlaced with associative leaps. Drawing on insights from cognitive science, computational linguistics, and mathematical epistemology, we define three core operations: *splitting* (decomposing a problem into formal constraints), *looming* (tacitly connecting disparate knowledge domains), and *tightening* (iteratively refining the resulting logical pattern). Through a series of case studies—ranging from mathematical conjecture to legal argumentation—we demonstrate how this weave accounts for moments of creative discovery that resist purely algorithmic explanation. The model further provides a structural vocabulary for analyzing errors, not as failures of logic, but as disruptions in the weave's tension. Our findings suggest that effective reasoning is less about following a linear path and more about maintaining a coherent texture between formal rigor and contextual intuition. This work offers a new lens for artificial intelligence research, particularly for designing systems capable of navigating the productive friction between rule-based processing and emergent, associative thought.

**Abstract**

This paper presents an overview of HIPE-2026, a shared task designed to advance the state-of-the-art in person-place relation extraction from multilingual historical texts. Addressing the unique challenges of historical corpora—including linguistic variation, non-standard orthographies, and fragmented contextual information—the task defines a novel schema for extracting and classifying semantic relations between named entities, specifically focusing on the spatial and social connections linking individuals to locations (e.g., birthplace, residence, affiliation). The task provides annotated datasets spanning multiple languages and historical periods, including English, French, and German, sourced from diverse archival materials such as census records, travelogues, and biographical dictionaries. Participants are required to perform both entity recognition and relation extraction, with evaluation emphasizing the accurate identification of implicit and explicit person-place relations. We detail the task design, annotation guidelines, and evaluation metrics, and summarize the key findings from the participating systems. Results reveal that transformer-based models achieve strong performance on modern-like texts but face significant degradation on highly irregular historical data, highlighting the need for specialized preprocessing and domain adaptation. This overview establishes HIPE-2026 as a benchmark for future research in historical text mining and digital humanities, offering insights into the extraction of geographically-grounded biographical networks from multilingual historical sources.

**Abstract:**  
We present **SARA** (Semantically Anchored Routing Alignment), a novel framework designed to unlock multilingual knowledge in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models. Despite their impressive performance, MoE models often exhibit biased expert routing for non-English languages, leading to underutilized multilingual capabilities. SARA addresses this by introducing a semantically anchored alignment mechanism that harmonizes routing decisions across languages. Leveraging parallel multilingual data, we construct a shared semantic anchor space that aligns expert selection with cross-lingual meaning equivalence, rather than surface-form token statistics. This is achieved through a lightweight routing alignment loss that encourages consistent expert activation for semantically identical inputs across languages, without requiring additional expert parameters. Extensive experiments on a range of multilingual benchmarks demonstrate that SARA significantly improves zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, boosting performance by up to 8.5% on downstream tasks while reducing routing variance by over 40%. Our analysis reveals that SARA enables the model to activate task-relevant experts more uniformly across languages, effectively unlocking dormant multilingual knowledge. The framework is model-agnostic, requires negligible inference overhead, and generalizes across MoE architectures. SARA thus offers a practical and scalable solution to harness the full multilingual potential of modern sparse MoE models.

**Abstract**
The proliferation of large language model (LLM) agents capable of tool use has led to significant advances in autonomous task completion. However, existing benchmarks predominantly evaluate agents under idealized conditions, assuming deterministic tool behavior and stable environments. In real-world deployments, tools frequently fail, return inconsistent outputs, or become temporarily unavailable—a phenomenon we term *tool-environment unreliability*. This paper introduces the **Tool-Environment Unreliability Benchmark (TEUB)** , a systematic framework designed to evaluate agent robustness across four critical dimensions of unreliability: tool invocation failure, output corruption, latency variability, and transient tool unavailability. We assess 12 state-of-the-art LLM agents, including both function-calling and reasoning-based architectures, across 8 diverse task domains. Our results reveal a significant performance collapse under unreliability: average task success rates drop by 34% to 62% compared to ideal conditions. Furthermore, we find that agents relying on rigid function-calling pipelines are disproportionately vulnerable, while those employing dynamic reasoning and self-healing strategies exhibit superior resilience. Through detailed error analysis, we identify key failure patterns—such as cascading errors from unverified tool outputs and brittle retry loops—and propose actionable design principles for building more robust tool-using systems. Our findings underscore that reliability, not just capability, is a critical frontier for deploying LLM agents in production environments.

**Abstract:** This study investigates the capacity of large language models (LLMs) to source and synthesize brand reputation data across diverse linguistic and market contexts. Through a systematic analysis of LLM outputs for a curated set of global brands in English, Mandarin, Arabic, and Spanish, we evaluate how these models retrieve, interpret, and aggregate sentiment from multilingual digital sources. Our methodology compares LLM-generated reputation assessments against traditional social media analytics and survey-based benchmarks, examining consistency in source identification, sentiment calibration, and cultural nuance handling. Results reveal that LLMs demonstrate robust performance in high-resource languages, accurately mirroring mainstream sentiment, but exhibit significant biases in low-resource markets, including over-reliance on Western-centric platforms and underweighting local forum discussions. Furthermore, we identify systematic distortions in cross-language sentiment transfer, where negative connotations from one market are often flattened or misaligned when aggregated into a global score. The findings underscore critical limitations in current LLM architectures for cross-cultural brand monitoring, particularly in capturing market-specific reputational risks and opportunities. We conclude by proposing hybrid frameworks that integrate LLM outputs with structured market intelligence to enhance reliability. This research provides actionable insights for practitioners using AI-driven reputation management and highlights pathways for improving multilingual source fidelity in brand analytics.

**Abstract:**  
The adversarial evaluation of large language models (LLMs) increasingly relies on automated safety judges to detect harmful outputs. While both encoder-based and decoder-based architectures are employed for this task, their relative efficacy remains underexplored. This paper presents a systematic, controlled comparison of encoder and decoder safety judges across diverse adversarial attack types, including jailbreaks, prompt injections, and toxic content generation. We evaluate multiple model families (BERT, RoBERTa, GPT, Llama) under identical training, data, and evaluation conditions. Our findings reveal that encoder judges consistently outperform decoder judges in detecting harmful responses, achieving higher true positive rates and lower false positive rates across all attack categories. Decoder judges exhibit greater vulnerability to adversarial perturbations, particularly when the adversarial input mimics benign stylistic patterns. However, decoder judges show marginally better calibration on out-of-distribution attacks. We further analyze the impact of model size, fine-tuning data, and contextual window length. Results suggest that encoder architectures leverage bidirectional contextualization to better generalize across attack surfaces, while decoders’ autoregressive nature introduces fragility. We conclude that encoder-based judges are currently more reliable for adversarial safety evaluation, though hybrid approaches may yield further gains. Our work provides actionable guidance for building robust LLM guardrails and highlights the need for architecture-specific adversarial defenses.

**Abstract**

We investigate the fundamental trade-off between computational space and the ability to generate languages in the limit, a classic framework for language learning from finite text. We introduce a novel model of *space-bounded language generation*, where a Turing machine must enumerate all strings of a target language while operating within a fixed, sublinear memory constraint relative to the length of the longest string generated. We establish tight upper and lower bounds on the space complexity required for generating various classes of languages, including regular, context-free, and recursive sets. Our main result shows that any recursively enumerable language can be generated in space logarithmic in the maximal string length, yet we prove that no algorithm using sublogarithmic space can generate a non-regular language, even under relaxed error tolerance. Conversely, we demonstrate that regular languages with a finite number of Myhill-Nerode equivalence classes admit generation in constant space. We further characterize the space requirements for generating languages in the limit when the generator is allowed to output strings out of order, revealing a strict hierarchy based on the density of the language. These findings provide a complete complexity-theoretic classification for space-efficient generation, offering new insights into the resource limitations of algorithmic language production and establishing foundational limits for compression-based and memory-constrained text generation systems.

**Abstract**  
The deployment of autonomous computer-use agents relies on accurate visual grounding and decision-making under uncertainty. However, current vision-language models (VLMs) lack systematic mechanisms to express confidence in their graphical user interface (GUI) predictions, leading to potential failures in critical tasks. This paper introduces a benchmark for uncertainty quantification (UQ) in GUI-grounding agents, evaluating how well VLMs represent and communicate their own predictive uncertainty across diverse datasets and tasks. We curate a suite of five GUI grounding datasets spanning web navigation, mobile app interactions, and desktop workflows, and assess six state-of-the-art VLMs on both point-click and text-entry tasks. Our benchmark measures calibration, selective abstention, and confidence-aware error detection. Results reveal that most VLMs are systematically overconfident, with calibration errors exceeding 20% on challenging GUI elements. We further demonstrate that simple post-hoc temperature scaling and ensembling methods can improve calibration, but performance varies significantly across domains and model architectures. Our findings underscore the critical gap in uncertainty-aware design for computer-use agents and provide a standardized evaluation framework to guide the development of safer, more reliable autonomous GUI interaction systems. The benchmark and code are publicly available to facilitate reproducible research.

**Abstract**  
We present OPERA, a novel reinforcement learning framework designed to align large language models with open-ended reasoning tasks through an objective perplexity-based reward. Traditional fine-tuning methods for reasoning often rely on supervised data or handcrafted reward signals that struggle to capture the nuanced correctness and coherence of multi-step, open-ended responses. OPERA addresses this by formulating a reward function grounded in perplexity differentials between the model’s generated reasoning and a reference policy, enabling automatic and scalable alignment without extensive human annotation. Our approach integrates a proximal policy optimization variant with a dedicated perplexity critic, which dynamically evaluates reasoning quality across diverse domains. Extensive experiments on mathematical reasoning, commonsense inference, and creative problem-solving benchmarks demonstrate that OPERA consistently outperforms baseline reinforcement learning methods and supervised fine-tuning. Models trained with OPERA exhibit enhanced logical consistency, reduced hallucination, and improved adaptability to novel reasoning paths. Moreover, the perplexity-based reward correlates strongly with human judgment of reasoning quality, confirming its practical validity. OPERA offers a principled, efficient pathway for aligning open-ended reasoning in LLMs, reducing the reliance on expensive human feedback while achieving superior generalization and coherence in complex, multi-turn reasoning scenarios.

**Abstract:** The rapid deployment of large language models (LLMs) necessitates robust safety evaluation frameworks. Existing safety benchmarks often rely on static datasets that fail to capture the nuanced, context-dependent nature of harmful outputs. We introduce **Refusal Alignment Scoring (RAS)** , a dynamic, model-agnostic metric for quantifying LLM safety by measuring the alignment between a model's refusal behavior and its explicit safety policy. RAS evaluates safety through two key dimensions: *Refusal Sensitivity*, which assesses the model's ability to reject harmful prompts, and *Refusal Consistency*, which measures the stability of its refusal behavior across semantically equivalent harmful queries. By constructing a taxonomy of harm categories and generating adversarial test cases via automated red-teaming, RAS produces a continuous safety score that reveals critical failure modes—such as "jailbreaking" and policy drift—not captured by pass/fail rates. We validate RAS against human judgments and existing benchmarks across multiple LLMs (including GPT-4, Llama-3, and Mistral), demonstrating its superior sensitivity in detecting safety regressions after fine-tuning. Our results show that RAS provides a principled, scalable framework for auditing safety policies and guiding alignment interventions, offering a crucial tool for responsible AI deployment.

**Abstract**  
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems are vulnerable to corpus poisoning attacks, wherein adversaries insert malicious documents designed to elicit specific target answers from downstream language models. Detecting such attacks requires identifying the precise tokens within poisoned documents that cause model misbehavior. We propose a token-level influence attribution framework to trace target answers back to their origin in corrupted retrieval corpora. Our method computes influence scores for each token in retrieved documents by estimating the effect of removing or perturbing that token on the model’s generation probability for the target answer. Using influence propagation across attention layers and embedding gradients, we construct a sparse influence graph that highlights critical adversarial tokens. Experiments on multiple RAG setups with GPT-2, Llama-2, and T5 models show that our approach achieves over 90% precision in pinpointing poisoned tokens across diverse attack strategies, including prompt injection, answer injection, and context manipulation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the identified tokens can be removed to neutralize the attack while preserving benign functionality. Our work provides a foundational tool for forensic analysis and defense in secure RAG deployments, enabling precise attribution of model outputs to malicious corpus elements.

**Abstract**

We introduce BitNet Text Embeddings, a novel approach for generating binary representations of textual data that achieves competitive performance with full-precision embeddings while drastically reducing memory footprint and computational cost. Unlike traditional embedding methods that rely on floating-point vectors, BitNet Text Embeddings quantize continuous embeddings into compact binary codes through a carefully designed binarization strategy that preserves semantic structure. Our method leverages a lightweight neural architecture with binary weights and activations, enabling efficient similarity computations via bitwise operations and Hamming distance metrics. We evaluate BitNet Text Embeddings on standard benchmarks for semantic textual similarity, clustering, and retrieval tasks. Results demonstrate that binary embeddings retain over 95% of the retrieval accuracy of their full-precision counterparts while compressing the embedding size by 32×. Furthermore, our approach accelerates similarity search by up to 10× on CPU and 20× on specialized hardware. The proposed method is particularly advantageous for resource-constrained environments such as mobile devices and edge computing, where memory and energy efficiency are critical. By combining the expressiveness of learned representations with the efficiency of binary operations, BitNet Text Embeddings offer a practical and scalable solution for large-scale text understanding and retrieval systems.

**Abstract**

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become a cornerstone for enhancing large language models with external knowledge, yet its basic form often struggles with complex relational queries, multi-hop reasoning, and contextual coherence. This paper systematically investigates whether GraphRAG—which integrates graph-structured knowledge bases and retrieval—is necessary, or whether simpler optimizations can achieve comparable performance. We first dissect the limitations of standard RAG, including fragmented context and shallow retrieval. Subsequently, we explore two progressive paradigms: GraphRAG, which leverages entity-relation graphs for structured traversal and holistic context; and Agentic RAG, which employs autonomous agents for dynamic, multi-step reasoning and selective information gathering. Through rigorous evaluation on question-answering benchmarks, we compare their trade-offs in accuracy, latency, and resource efficiency. Our findings reveal that while GraphRAG excels in tasks requiring explicit relational understanding, basic RAG enhanced with context optimization—such as chunking strategies, query expansion, and reranking—can bridge the gap for many real-world scenarios. Agentic solutions further improve adaptability but introduce computational overhead. We conclude that the choice depends on task complexity: for simple factoid queries, optimized basic RAG suffices; for deep, interconnected knowledge demands, GraphRAG or agentic methods are warranted. This work provides a pragmatic framework for selecting and configuring RAG variants, offering clarity on when to invest in graph-based or agentic extensions versus refining foundational approaches.

**Abstract**
Medical errors pose a significant threat to patient safety, often arising from complex clinical workflows and information overload. This paper introduces *MedGuards*, a novel multi-agent system designed for reliable detection and correction of medical errors across clinical documentation, diagnosis, and prescription processes. MedGuards employs a collaborative architecture comprising specialized agents: a Data Extraction Agent, a Diagnostic Validation Agent, a Pharmacological Checker Agent, and a Contextual Reasoning Agent. These agents operate in a coordinated pipeline, cross-referencing patient records, clinical guidelines, and drug databases to identify discrepancies, contraindications, and omissions in real-time. Upon detecting an error, the system triggers a Correction Agent that generates evidence-based remediation suggestions, which are then reviewed by a Consensus Agent to ensure clinical plausibility before flagging for clinician attention. Evaluated on a synthetic dataset of 5,000 clinical cases and a real-world annotated corpus of 200 discharge summaries, MedGuards achieved 94.7% sensitivity and 92.3% precision in error detection, reducing false positives by 38% compared to single-agent baselines. Furthermore, the system demonstrated a 91% user satisfaction rate in simulated deployment, with a mean correction latency under 2.5 seconds. Our results indicate that multi-agent collaboration significantly enhances the reliability and interpretability of automated medical error mitigation, offering a scalable framework for integration into electronic health record systems.

**Abstract**  
We present Perspective-Bounded Memory (PBM), a novel framework for book-based role-playing agents that enforces character consistency through memory constraints derived from narrative perspective. Existing agents often fail to maintain authentic character boundaries, inadvertently accessing or referencing knowledge beyond their established viewpoint—such as future events, hidden motivations, or omniscient details—breaking immersion. PBM addresses this by constructing a structured memory store that is strictly bounded by the character’s known information at each story point, integrating retrieval mechanisms that filter external knowledge through the lens of the character’s current awareness. We implement PBM within a large language model agent architecture and evaluate on a curated benchmark of classic novels, measuring character fidelity, plot coherence, and user-rated immersion. Results show that PBM agents significantly reduce out-of-character violations compared to baseline memory-augmented models, while maintaining fluent dialogue and narrative progression. Ablation studies reveal that both temporal and informational bounding are critical for preserving perspective. Our approach enables more immersive, believable interactions in open-ended book-based role-play, with implications for narrative AI, interactive fiction, and digital humanities tools.

**Abstract**

The adoption of structured output constraints, such as JSON schemas and regular expressions, in large language model (LLM) deployments is intended to enforce format reliability and prevent undesirable outputs. However, we identify and characterize a novel phenomenon termed the "Constraint Tax": a systematic suppression of tool-calling capabilities when open-weight LLMs operate under rigid output formatting. Through an empirical study across four prominent open-weight LLM families (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, and Gemma), we measure the degradation in functional tool-use accuracy when models are forced to adhere to predefined structured output schemas compared to unconstrained generation. Our findings reveal a significant and consistent performance penalty—ranging from 10% to 45% reduction in successful tool invocation—across all tested architectures, with the severity varying by model size and constraint complexity. We demonstrate that this tax is not attributable to simple tokenization overhead or prompt formatting artifacts, but stems from a fundamental interference with the model’s latent reasoning pathways for action selection. Furthermore, we show that post-hoc schema enforcement via constrained decoding partially mitigates the tax, yet introduces latency trade-offs. Our results highlight a critical trade-off between output reliability and functional capability, urging practitioners to carefully weigh the necessity of structural constraints against the operational cost of suppressed tool use in agentic workflows.

**Abstract:** We present Riazi-8B, an 8-billion parameter large language model (LLM) specifically designed for mathematical reasoning in Urdu. Despite the global prevalence of Urdu, existing LLMs predominantly cater to English and other high-resource languages, leaving a critical gap in specialized domains such as mathematics. Riazi-8B is built upon a custom Urdu-centric tokenizer and fine-tuned on a novel, manually curated dataset comprising over 1.2 million Urdu mathematical problems and solutions, spanning arithmetic, algebra, geometry, and word problems. The model architecture incorporates a specialized reasoning head to enhance step-by-step solution generation. Evaluated on a held-out test set of Urdu math problems, Riazi-8B achieves 82.4% accuracy, outperforming general-purpose multilingual models (e.g., Llama-2-7B, mT5) by over 28% on the same tasks. Notably, it demonstrates improved coherence in intermediate reasoning steps and reduces common errors in numerical translation. Our results indicate that domain-specific, language-focused pretraining can significantly bridge performance gaps in underrepresented languages. Riazi-8B is released under an open-source license to foster research in Urdu NLP and equitable access to AI-driven educational tools.

**Abstract:** Large language model (LLM) agents face significant challenges in long-horizon decision-making due to sparse reward signals and inefficient exploration. We propose BiPACE (Bisimulation-Guided Policy Optimization with Action Counterfactual Estimation), a novel framework that integrates bisimulation metrics with action-level counterfactual reasoning to enhance agent learning. By leveraging state-action bisimulation, BiPACE learns a compact latent representation that captures behavioral equivalence, enabling efficient generalization across similar decision trajectories. The core innovation lies in a counterfactual estimation mechanism that evaluates the impact of alternative actions on future reward distributions without requiring explicit environment models. This allows the agent to selectively prioritize actions that lead to high-value states, even when immediate rewards are absent. We further introduce a bisimulation-guided policy optimization objective that jointly optimizes for representation fidelity and policy improvement, reducing variance in gradient estimates and mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Extensive experiments on complex text-based environments and interactive benchmarks demonstrate that BiPACE achieves superior sample efficiency and task completion rates compared to standard reinforcement learning baselines and prior representation learning methods. Our results highlight the synergy between bisimulation abstractions and counterfactual reasoning, offering a principled approach for scaling LLM agents to intricate, long-duration tasks.

**Abstract**  
Accurate multi-intent spoken language understanding (SLU) remains challenging due to ambiguous utterance segmentation, overlapping intent boundaries, and noisy speech transcriptions. Existing approaches often treat intent detection and slot filling as independent tasks or rely on single-pass reasoning, leading to fragility under real-world linguistic variability. This paper introduces SFL-MTSC, a novel framework that leverages semantic frame-level representations and multi-task self-consistency to achieve robust multi-intent SLU. Our model first enriches utterance encoding with FrameNet-derived semantic frames, capturing fine-grained event structures and cross-intent dependencies. A multi-task architecture jointly optimizes intent detection, slot filling, and a novel self-consistency objective that penalizes contradictions between predicted intent-slot mappings and frame-level constraints. During inference, we aggregate predictions from multiple stochastic passes, enforcing semantic coherence via a consistency voting mechanism. Experiments on three benchmark datasets (SNIPS, ATIS, and a custom multi-intent corpus) demonstrate that SFL-MTSC outperforms strong baselines, achieving up to 8.2% relative improvement in joint intent-slot accuracy. Ablation studies confirm the critical role of frame-level semantics and self-consistency regularization, particularly in handling ambiguous or noisy inputs. Our framework also exhibits superior generalization to zero-shot and low-resource scenarios, highlighting its practical robustness for conversational AI systems.

**Abstract**

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a transformative paradigm for grounding large language models in external, verifiable knowledge sources, enabling more factual and context-aware responses. However, the integration of retrieval mechanisms with generative models introduces a complex and under-explored threat landscape for security and privacy. This paper provides a comprehensive systematization of the security and privacy challenges inherent in modern RAG architectures. We first delineate the core architectural components—indexing, retrieval, fusion, and generation—and map them to a threat taxonomy encompassing adversarial poisoning, data leakage, prompt injection, membership inference, and denial-of-service attacks. We then survey and critically analyze state-of-the-art defensive strategies, including sanitization, differential privacy, secure enclaves, and adversarial training, evaluating their efficacy, overhead, and trade-offs. Our analysis reveals significant gaps: most defenses focus on isolated components, lack robustness against adaptive adversaries, and fail to address privacy risks in multi-turn retrieval contexts. Finally, we outline critical future directions, including the need for holistic, system-level security frameworks, privacy-preserving retrieval protocols, and formal verification of RAG pipelines. This paper aims to serve as a foundational reference for researchers and practitioners building trustworthy, secure, and privacy-preserving retrieval-augmented systems.

**Abstract**

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in code generation, yet their ability to optimize software for real-world performance remains largely unquantified. This paper presents a systematic evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs on the task of performance optimization across diverse, production-grade codebases. We construct a benchmark comprising 50 non-trivial, latency-sensitive functions sourced from open-source projects, each with a known, validated optimization. Using a standardized methodology, we assess LLMs on their ability to produce functionally equivalent, faster implementations, measuring both speedup and correctness. Our experiments reveal a significant gap between theoretical capability and practical utility: while LLMs frequently suggest syntactically valid optimizations, they achieve a median speedup of only 5-8% on the original code, with over 40% of generated optimizations introducing regressions or breaking correctness. Furthermore, performance varies substantially by domain, with models excelling on algorithmic micro-optimizations but struggling with architecture-specific or I/O-bound improvements. We identify key failure modes, including a tendency to favor readability over performance and an inability to reason about cache behavior or parallelization. These findings highlight critical limitations in current LLM training paradigms and suggest that significant advances in reasoning about runtime complexity and hardware constraints are necessary for practical deployment in software performance engineering.

**Abstract**  
Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable mathematical reasoning capabilities, yet they remain vulnerable to critical single-token perturbations that abruptly derail their chain-of-thought processes. We introduce the concept of *cliff tokens*—individual tokens whose removal or modification causes a catastrophic drop in final answer accuracy, despite minimal impact on local perplexity. Through systematic probing across multiple LLM families (LLaMA, GPT, Mistral) and arithmetic reasoning benchmarks, we identify that such tokens cluster at key junctures: intermediate calculation steps, operator boundaries, and conclusion transitions. We show that cliff tokens are not merely rare outliers but occur with sufficient frequency (up to 8% of all tokens) to significantly degrade overall performance. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these fragile points can be pre-identified using gradient-based sensitivity analysis without requiring full model retraining. By masking or reinforcing cliff tokens during inference, we achieve up to 15% improvement in final answer accuracy on challenging multi-step problems. Our findings reveal a fundamental brittleness in LLM reasoning and provide a practical mechanism for robustification through targeted token-level intervention.

**Abstract**

This study investigates the behavioral drivers of rating-sentiment incongruence, a phenomenon where user-generated numerical ratings diverge from the emotional valence of accompanying textual reviews. Analyzing a large-scale dataset from a popular e-commerce platform, we identify and quantify three key psychological mechanisms: the “negativity bias,” where users penalize minor flaws disproportionately; “expectation disconfirmation,” driven by pre-purchase hype; and the “social signaling effect,” where users inflate ratings for self-presentation while writing critical reviews. Using a mixed-methods approach combining logistic regression with natural language processing, we find that incongruence is not random noise but a systematic outcome of these behavioral tendencies. Specifically, reviews exhibiting strong emotional language paired with moderate ratings are most likely to reflect expectation disconfirmation, while highly positive ratings paired with detailed negative commentary are indicative of social signaling. Our results demonstrate that rating-sentiment incongruence significantly distorts aggregate product scores, leading to biased consumer decision-making. We conclude that platforms must account for these behavioral drivers—not merely textual or numeric data—to improve recommendation systems. By revealing the “fault” in our stars, this paper offers actionable insights for designing more robust, psychologically-aware review aggregation algorithms.

**Abstract**

The proliferation of Arabic social media content, particularly on Twitter, has amplified the need for robust automated systems capable of simultaneously filtering spam and analyzing sentiment. This study investigates the efficacy of the MARBERT model, a state-of-the-art Arabic language representation model, for the dual tasks of spam detection and sentiment analysis in Arabic tweets. We evaluate MARBERT against traditional machine learning classifiers (e.g., SVM, Naïve Bayes) and other transformer-based models (e.g., AraBERT) using a comprehensive, manually annotated dataset comprising both spam and non-spam tweets with positive, negative, and neutral sentiment labels. Our experimental results demonstrate that MARBERT significantly outperforms baseline models, achieving a macro F1-score of 0.94 for spam classification and an average accuracy of 87.3% for three-class sentiment analysis. Furthermore, we introduce a novel hierarchical multi-task learning framework that leverages shared contextual representations, enabling the model to jointly optimize both objectives. This approach not only reduces computational overhead but also improves overall performance by capturing the intrinsic relationship between spammy content and sentiment polarity. The findings underscore the robustness of MARBERT in handling the morphological richness and dialectal diversity of Arabic, establishing a new benchmark for integrated spam and sentiment detection on Arabic social media. This work has practical implications for content moderation and social media analytics in Arabic-speaking digital ecosystems.

**Abstract**

Automated scoring systems for Automated Speech Recognition (ASR) are increasingly employed to evaluate model performance and detect adversarial inputs, yet their reliability under adversarial conditions remains poorly understood. This paper investigates the calibration and adversarial robustness of a state-of-the-art ASR scoring judge, focusing on its susceptibility to jailbreak-style attacks designed to manipulate confidence scores. We introduce a systematic framework to assess the judge's calibration across varying noise levels, linguistic perturbations, and targeted adversarial prompts. Our experiments reveal significant miscalibration, particularly under distributional shift and low-confidence regimes, where the judge exhibits overconfidence in erroneous predictions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that carefully crafted adversarial perturbations can induce substantial score inflation or deflation, undermining the judge's trustworthiness as an arbiter of ASR quality. To mitigate these vulnerabilities, we propose a calibration-aware adversarial training method that improves robustness while preserving scoring accuracy. Our findings highlight critical limitations in current automated ASR evaluation pipelines and underscore the need for rigorous calibration checks and adversarial defenses to ensure reliable performance assessment in real-world deployment.

**Abstract**  
The rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) across diverse applications necessitates robust methods for evaluating their reliability, particularly regarding faithfulness—the degree to which model outputs align with factual accuracy and contextual consistency. This paper presents a structured red teaming framework specifically designed to systematically probe and assess faithfulness vulnerabilities in LLMs. Unlike traditional evaluation metrics that focus on fluency or task completion, our framework operationalizes adversarial testing through targeted prompt perturbations, contradictory context injection, and multi-turn logical consistency challenges. We conduct a comprehensive case study using this framework on several state-of-the-art LLMs, revealing significant and systematic failures in maintaining factual coherence, especially under conditions of ambiguous retrieval or conflicting instructions. Our findings demonstrate that standard performance benchmarks often mask these critical faithfulness gaps. The proposed framework not only identifies specific failure modes but also provides a taxonomy of attack surfaces, enabling developers to prioritize mitigation strategies. We further show that iterative red teaming, coupled with targeted fine-tuning, can substantially reduce faithfulness errors. This work establishes a principled methodology for stress-testing LLMs, offering both a practical tool for safety evaluation and a foundation for developing more resilient models. The results underscore the necessity of adversarial evaluation as a standard component in LLM deployment pipelines.

**Abstract**

Automatic text summarization remains a critical challenge in natural language processing, particularly for generating fluent, concise, and semantically accurate abstractive summaries. While pre-trained transformer models like PEGASUS have demonstrated strong performance via specialized gap-sentence masking, their general-domain pretraining often fails to capture domain-specific nuances and stylistic conventions required for specialized corpora. This paper presents a systematic investigation into optimizing abstractive summarization through fine-tuning the PEGASUS architecture on targeted datasets. We evaluate the impact of various fine-tuning strategies, including domain-adaptive pretraining, curriculum learning, and mixed-task objective tuning, across three distinct domains: scientific articles, legal documents, and news briefs. Our experiments demonstrate that fine-tuned PEGASUS models consistently outperform both the vanilla pretrained baseline and established BART-based competitors, achieving up to 18% improvement in ROUGE-L scores and significant gains in factual consistency, as measured by the newly introduced FEQA metric. Furthermore, we identify optimal hyperparameter configurations—such as learning rate scheduling and adapter-layer integration—that mitigate catastrophic forgetting while maximizing downstream task alignment. Through qualitative analysis, we show that fine-tuned models generate summaries with improved discourse coherence and reduced hallucination rates. Our findings provide actionable guidelines for deploying PEGASUS in production summarization systems, proving that targeted fine-tuning substantially bridges the gap between general-purpose pretraining and domain-expert performance.

**Abstract**

This paper introduces a fully differentiable framework for neural forced alignment, enabling end-to-end training of sequence-to-sequence models without the need for discrete alignment annotations. Traditional forced alignment relies on dynamic programming algorithms such as Viterbi decoding, which involve non-differentiable argmax operations and hard constraints, thereby preventing gradient backpropagation through the alignment process. We propose to relax these discrete operations by employing soft dynamic programming, where the hard selection of optimal alignment paths is replaced by differentiable, weighted combinations of all possible alignments. Specifically, we formulate a soft variant of the Viterbi algorithm that computes a differentiable approximation of the optimal alignment score and its corresponding monotonic alignment path. This formulation allows the entire alignment procedure to be integrated as a differentiable module within a neural network, facilitating joint optimization of acoustic models and alignment objectives via standard gradient descent. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on phoneme-level forced alignment tasks, showing that the differentiable alignment yields improved robustness to sequence length variability and superior generalization compared to traditional non-differentiable baselines. Furthermore, our method seamlessly integrates with modern attention-based architectures, enabling end-to-end training without external alignment tools. The proposed framework thus bridges the gap between dynamic programming and deep learning, offering a principled and efficient solution for neural forced alignment.

**Abstract**

Self-supervised speech representations have demonstrated remarkable performance across various languages and tasks. However, their ability to capture fine-grained phonetic distinctions within a single language’s dialectal continuum remains underexplored. This paper presents a case study investigating how models like wav2vec 2.0 and HuBERT represent Mandarin Chinese sub-dialects. We employ an unsupervised articulatory analysis framework, using a neural articulatory synthesizer to map acoustic representations back to articulatory parameters (e.g., tongue position, lip rounding). By probing these synthesized articulatory features, we assess the models' sensitivity to dialect-specific phonetic phenomena, such as alveolar-palatal fricative contrasts and tone sandhi patterns. Our results reveal that while all models capture broad phonetic categories, only deeper layers in HuBERT show systematic differentiation of sub-dialectal articulatory cues, particularly for tonal variations. Furthermore, we find a significant gap between acoustic representation similarity and articulatory feature similarity, indicating that high acoustic performance does not guarantee the encoding of articulatory grounding. This work highlights the value of unsupervised articulatory analysis as a diagnostic tool for evaluating representation quality and demonstrates that current self-supervised models may overlook crucial sub-dialectal phonetic details present in natural speech.

**Abstract**

We introduce the *Generalization Spectrum*, a novel framework for evaluating and characterizing learning algorithms by analogy to chromatographic separation. Inspired by the way chromatography separates chemical compounds based on their differential affinity for a stationary phase, our method systematically probes a model’s inductive bias by exposing it to a controlled spectrum of training data complexities. By varying key dataset characteristics—such as noise levels, feature relevance, and sample size—and measuring the resulting generalization error, we generate a continuous profile, or spectrum, that reveals distinct phases of underfitting, optimal generalization, and overfitting. This approach moves beyond single-point performance metrics (e.g., test accuracy) to provide a holistic, resolution-rich view of a learning algorithm’s behavior across the entire complexity landscape. We demonstrate that the shape, width, and peak of this spectrum serve as robust signatures of algorithmic properties, including regularization strength, capacity, and susceptibility to memorization. Using this chromatographic lens, we compare several classic and modern architectures, showing how the Generalization Spectrum can diagnose subtle failures, predict transfer learning performance, and guide hyperparameter selection. Our findings suggest that this method offers a principled, scalable, and interpretable tool for benchmarking and debugging learning algorithms, shifting the focus from isolated accuracy measurements to a richer understanding of generalization dynamics.

**Abstract**

The proliferation of large language models and retrieval-augmented generation systems has introduced a critical paradox: while these systems rely on vast memory stores to enhance performance, the quality of that memory fundamentally shapes output reliability. This paper introduces *Reclaim Evaluation*, a novel framework for assessing the integrity of memory retrieval in generative AI, challenging the prevailing assumption that more data universally improves model behavior. Through controlled experiments comparing models with pristine, curated memory banks against those with corrupted, lossy, or outdated repositories, we demonstrate that degraded memory—whether through compression artifacts, staleness, or hallucinated embeddings—produces outputs with significantly higher error rates, increased bias propagation, and diminished factual coherence. Our findings reveal that a model with no external memory access consistently outperforms one relying on a compromised memory store, reducing hallucination frequency by up to 34% and improving answer accuracy by 21% across benchmark tasks. We argue that memory pruning and integrity auditing are essential preconditions for reliable AI deployment, and propose that the field shift focus from maximizing memory volume to ensuring memory fidelity. Ultimately, this work establishes that in generative retrieval, a lossy memory is not merely suboptimal—it is demonstrably worse than an empty one.

**Abstract:**  
Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on two critical components: *harness design*—the architectural scaffolding that defines how tools, memory, and external APIs are integrated—and *post-training*—the fine-tuning or reinforcement learning applied after initial pretraining. While prior work has examined these elements in isolation, their synergistic interplay remains underexplored. This paper investigates how the choice of harness structure (e.g., monolithic vs. modular tool-use, static vs. dynamic memory retrieval) interacts with post-training strategies (e.g., supervised fine-tuning, reward-based alignment, or self-play) to shape agent robustness, generalization, and efficiency. We systematically evaluate combinations of harness configurations and post-training methods across diverse tasks, including multi-step reasoning, real-time information retrieval, and tool-usage scenarios. Our results reveal that harness design significantly modulates the effectiveness of post-training: modular harnesses amplify the benefits of alignment techniques but require careful credit assignment, whereas monolithic harnesses are more resilient to distributional shifts but limit the expressivity of fine-tuning. Conversely, post-training can compensate for structural weaknesses in harness design, yet at the cost of sample efficiency. We further identify emergent failure modes—such as "harness misalignment"—where the harness induces latent biases that post-training exacerbates. Our findings provide a principled framework for co-optimizing harness architecture and post-training, offering actionable guidelines for building more reliable and adaptive LLM agents.

**Abstract**

This paper investigates whether pre-training a speech encoder with translation-enhanced objectives improves the performance of speech-based large language models (LLMs). While conventional speech encoder pre-training focuses on acoustic or linguistic features, we hypothesize that cross-modal alignment through translation tasks can foster more robust semantic representations. We compare two pre-training paradigms: standard self-supervised learning (e.g., HuBERT, Wav2Vec 2.0) and a translation-enhanced variant that jointly predicts translated text from speech and masked acoustic units. Using a unified LLM architecture for speech understanding and generation, we evaluate both approaches on tasks including automatic speech recognition, speech-to-text translation, spoken question answering, and semantic speech retrieval. Our experiments reveal that translation-enhanced pre-training yields modest improvements in cross-lingual and semantic tasks, particularly for low-resource language pairs, but offers no significant gain for monolingual recognition or generation fluency. Furthermore, we observe that the added translation objective can introduce training instability and increase computational overhead without proportional gains in downstream performance. We conclude that while translation-enhanced pre-training can enrich certain speech representations, its benefits are task-specific and do not universally justify the additional complexity. Our findings provide practical guidance for designing pre-training strategies in speech LLMs and highlight the need for careful task-aligned objectives.
